label.reasoning: The item asks how a protein distinguishes between two monosaccharides (glucose and mannose) that have the same chemical formula but different structural orientations. This requires understanding how structural differences (isomers) affect macromolecular interactions and shape-specific binding (Topic 1.4).
The question requires applying the concept of structural isomerism in carbohydrates (Unit 1) to explain how structural shape affects protein-ligand binding specificity in membrane transport (Unit 2).

The question requires applying the concept of carbohydrate structure and isomerism to explain how a minor structural difference (hydroxyl group orientation) alters the 3D shape of the monosaccharide, preventing it from fitting into a specific protein binding site.

The question requires applying concepts of macromolecule structure (isomers and shape) from Unit 1 to explain how membrane transport proteins exhibit specificity (Unit 2, facilitated diffusion). The student must recognize that a difference in the orientation of a single hydroxyl group alters the overall shape of the sugar, preventing it from fitting the transport protein's binding site.

The question requires the student to compare the structural features of two cells (such as presence/absence of a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles) to classify them as prokaryotic or eukaryotic, applying core concepts of cell compartmentalization.

The item requires the student to apply knowledge of structural differences between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells (specifically the presence or absence of a nuclear envelope/nucleus and membrane-bound organelles) to classify two newly described single-celled organisms, representing a single-step application of a concept to a new scenario.

The question requires applying the distinguishing characteristics of prokaryotes and eukaryotes, such as membrane-bound organelles, to classify two cells. This aligns with Topic 2.9 (Cell Compartmentalization), which contrasts prokaryotic and eukaryotic internal organization. The difficulty is Medium because students must interpret the stimulus descriptions and apply classification concepts.

The student must apply the mechanism of co-translational targeting to the ER (described in the stimulus) to a novel scenario where a cytosolic enzyme is engineered with an ER signal peptide. Predicting that this modification will redirect the enzyme into the ER lumen requires applying basic organelle function concepts.

The student must apply the mechanism of cotranslation targeting to the rough ER, described in the stimulus, to predict the outcome of adding an ER signal peptide to a cytoplasmic enzyme. This requires single-step reasoning from the provided premises.

The student must apply the structural differences between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells (specifically the presence of a nuclear envelope and membrane-bound organelles in eukaryotes versus their absence in prokaryotes) to classify the two described organisms.
